summary: Describes the ARIA encryption algorithm, a block cipher that works on 128-bit blocks and supports 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys. It consists of a key scheduling part and a data randomizing part. This is an informational description, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: ARIA is a secret code machine that scrambles messages in chunks using a key, and this document explains how it is built.

subtitle: A Korean 128-bit block cipher with 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys, described step by step.

tldr.problem: ARIA is a block cipher developed by Korean cryptographers and used in Korea, and implementers elsewhere needed a written description of the algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: ARIA encrypts 128-bit blocks in 12, 14 or 16 rounds depending on key size, using a key schedule built from a 3-round Feistel construction and rounds made of S-box substitution layers and a fixed diffusion layer.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an informational description, not a standard, and its appendices provide test vectors and ASN.1 object identifiers for ARIA modes of operation.

facts.label: S-boxes
facts.value: 4 (SB1 to SB4), 8 bits in and out

today: RFC 5794 is an Informational document from the Independent Submission stream, so it is not an Internet Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC Editor states it makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: What ARIA Is
sections.content:
ARIA is a general-purpose block cipher developed by Korean cryptographers in 2003. It is an iterated block cipher with 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys that encrypts 128-bit blocks in 12, 14 and 16 rounds, depending on the key size. The RFC says it suits most software and hardware implementations on 32-bit and 8-bit processors.

It was established as a Korean standard block cipher algorithm in 2004 and, according to the document, has been widely used in Korea, especially for government-to-public services. It was included in PKCS #11 in 2007. The algorithm has two parts: a key scheduling part and a data randomizing part.
sections.plainLanguage: ARIA is a lock that scrambles messages in 16-byte pieces. A longer key means a stronger lock, and the lock uses more twisting steps.

sections.title: The Key Schedule
sections.content:
The master key K is 128, 192 or 256 bits. It is split into two 128-bit values, KL (the leftmost 128 bits) and KR (the rest, right-padded with zeros). Four 128-bit values W0 to W3 are then computed as the intermediate values of a 3-round, 256-bit Feistel cipher run on KL || KR, using constants CK1, CK2 and CK3. These constants are rotations of three values C1, C2 and C3 depending on key size, and come from the first 128*3 bits of the fractional part of 1/PI.

From W0 to W3 the schedule produces encryption round keys ek1 to ek17 using XORs and circular rotations by 19, 31 and 61 bits. An extra key addition layer in the last round means 12-, 14- and 16-round versions need 13, 15 and 17 round keys. Decryption round keys are derived from the encryption round keys, in reverse order, with the diffusion layer applied to all but the first and last.
sections.plainLanguage: The schedule takes your one secret key and stirs it into a whole set of smaller keys, one for each twisting step of the lock.

sections.title: Encrypting and Decrypting a Block
sections.content:
Encryption takes a 128-bit plaintext and applies the round functions in turn. Odd rounds use FO and even rounds use FE, each with the next round key. The last round is different: it applies the type 2 substitution layer to the data XORed with the second-to-last round key, then XORs the final round key. The three key sizes follow the same pattern with 12, 14 or 16 rounds.

Decryption is the same process as encryption, except that the encryption round keys are replaced by the decryption round keys. No separate decryption circuit is described.
sections.plainLanguage: To lock a block you run it through the same twisting steps in order. To unlock it you run the same steps with the keys prepared in backward order.

sections.title: Round Functions, S-boxes and Diffusion
sections.content:
Each round function mixes the data with the round key RK, substitutes bytes and diffuses the result: FO(D,RK) = A(SL1(D ^ RK)) and FE(D,RK) = A(SL2(D ^ RK)). The two substitution layers, SL1 and SL2, alternate between rounds. Each takes a 16-byte string and runs every byte through one of four 8-bit-to-8-bit S-boxes, SB1 to SB4. The RFC prints all four as lookup tables. SB3 and SB4 are the inverses of SB1 and SB2, so SL2 is the inverse of SL1.

The diffusion layer A takes 16 bytes and outputs 16 bytes, where each output byte is the XOR of seven input bytes. The RFC notes that A is an involution: applying it twice returns the original input.
sections.plainLanguage: Each twist swaps every byte using a lookup chart, then shuffles all the bytes together so a tiny change spreads everywhere.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that ARIA is designed to be resistant to all known attacks on block ciphers. It also says its security was analyzed by the COSIC group of K.U.Leuven in Belgium and that no security flaw was found. These are claims made by the document's authors, which cites their design paper and the Leuven evaluation as sources.
sections.plainLanguage: The makers say the lock resists every known way of picking it, and a lab in Belgium checked it and found no flaw.

sections.title: Test Data and Object Identifiers
sections.content:
Appendix A gives example data in hexadecimal. For a 128-bit key 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f and plaintext 00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff, the ciphertext is d718fbd6ab644c739da95f3be6451778, with all round keys and intermediate values listed. Shorter examples are given for 192- and 256-bit keys.

Appendix B provides an ASN.1 module defining object identifiers and parameter structures for ARIA in many modes of operation: ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR for confidentiality, CMAC for authentication, and OCB 2.0, GCM, CCM and Key Wrap for combined or wrapping uses, each for the three key sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendices give an answer key, so you can check your own ARIA machine against the official results.
